lede: A vector written in components tells you how far across and how far up. Two questions are usually asked of it instead: how long is the arrow, and which way does it point. Both answers come out of the right-angled triangle the components make.
can: Find the magnitude of a vector with Pythagoras, whatever the signs of its components
Find the angle a vector makes with i or with j, and check the pair adds to 90 degrees
Build the vector the question means first, then give its size and its direction

caption: The force $(6\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ N: two components at right angles, and the arrow they build.

md: The $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ directions are at right angles, so the two components and the arrow make a right-angled triangle, with the arrow as its hypotenuse. Pythagoras gives its length, the **magnitude**: $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ for $x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}$, printed on the formula sheet.
A minus sign changes nothing, because $(-6)^2$ is $36$, the same as $6^2$. The magnitude is never the sum of the components, and never the larger one on its own.

stem: A force $\mathbf{F} = (6\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ N. Calculate the magnitude of $\mathbf{F}$, to 2 decimal places.

steps.decision: The components are at right angles, so the arrow is the hypotenuse: square each, add, and root. This line with the numbers in earns the method mark.
Root the sum and round to 2 decimal places. The value earns the working mark, and the newton stays: the magnitude of a force is a force.

prompt: What is the magnitude of $(5\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j})$ N, to 2 decimal places, in newtons?
explain: Square each component, add, and root, as in step 1 of See it: $\sqrt{5^2 + 9^2} = \sqrt{106} = 10.30$ N. Adding the components gives 14, longer than the arrow; stopping at 106 leaves out the root.

twin.prompt: What is the magnitude of $(-6\mathbf{i} + 11\mathbf{j})$ N, to 2 decimal places, in newtons?
twin.explain: The minus sign goes when the component is squared: $\sqrt{(-6)^2 + 11^2} = \sqrt{157} = 12.53$ N.

caption: The angle with $\mathbf{i}$: the $\mathbf{j}$ component is opposite it, the $\mathbf{i}$ component beside it.

md: The angle with $\mathbf{i}$ sits at the start of the arrow, between it and the x-axis. The $\mathbf{j}$ component is opposite that angle and the $\mathbf{i}$ component is beside it, so $\tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x}$ and $\theta = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{y}{x}$, the second formula on the sheet.

title: Summer 2025, Question 2(iii)
md: The commonest error on the angle was the reciprocal of the ratio needed, as it was in Summer 2019, although the right formula is printed on the sheet. Sketch the triangle and mark the angle before you reach for the calculator.

stem: Calculate the angle $\mathbf{F} = (6\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ N makes with the positive x-axis, to 2 decimal places.

steps.decision: The angle is at the x-axis: the j component, 5, is opposite it and the i component, 6, is beside it. This line earns the method mark.
Calculator in degrees, then 2 decimal places. 5 is less than 6, so the arrow is flatter than 45°: an angle under 45° agrees.

title: Magnitude and Direction
why: The same two calculations at a slower pace. Watch the triangle being sketched before the calculator comes out: that is the habit that keeps the fraction the right way up.

prompt: What angle does $(3\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j})$ make with the positive x-axis, to 2 decimal places, in degrees?
explain: Put the $\mathbf{j}$ component over the $\mathbf{i}$ component, as in step 1 of See it: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{7}{3} = 66.80^{\circ}$, steeper than 45° because 7 is more than 3. The fraction turned over gives $23.20^{\circ}$, the angle with $\mathbf{j}$.

twin.prompt: What angle does $(7\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ make with the positive x-axis, to 2 decimal places, in degrees?
twin.explain: The $\mathbf{j}$ component over the $\mathbf{i}$ component: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2}{7} = 15.95^{\circ}$, a shallow arrow because 2 is much less than 7.

caption: One arrow, two angles: one from $\mathbf{i}$, one from $\mathbf{j}$. Together they fill the quarter turn.

md: Measure from $\mathbf{j}$ instead and the components swap roles: the $\mathbf{i}$ component is now opposite the angle, so the angle with $\mathbf{j}$ is $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x}{y}$. It is not on the sheet, but the two angles always add to $90^{\circ}$.
When $\mathbf{i}$ points east and $\mathbf{j}$ points north, a bearing is measured clockwise from north, so it is the angle with $\mathbf{j}$, written with three figures before the point.

title: Why the two angles make 90°
md: The two axes meet at a right angle, and the arrow splits that quarter turn into two pieces. So one angle is whatever the other leaves of $90^{\circ}$, and a fraction the wrong way up shows at once.

stem: For $\mathbf{F} = (6\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ N, find the angle it makes with $\mathbf{j}$. Then, with $\mathbf{i}$ east and $\mathbf{j}$ north, give its bearing.

steps.decision: From j, the i component, 6, is opposite and the j component, 5, is beside, so the fraction turns over.
The angle with i from the section above and this one fill the quarter turn, so the fraction is the right way up.
A bearing starts at north and turns clockwise, which is the angle with j when j points north, written with three figures.

prompt: What angle does $(2\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ make with $\mathbf{j}$, to 2 decimal places, in degrees?
explain: From $\mathbf{j}$ the $\mathbf{i}$ component is opposite, so the fraction is $x$ over $y$, as in step 1 of See it: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2}{5} = 21.80^{\circ}$. The angle with $\mathbf{i}$ is $68.20^{\circ}$, and the two add to $90^{\circ}$.

twin.prompt: What angle does $(3\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j})$ make with $\mathbf{j}$, to 2 decimal places, in degrees?
twin.explain: $x$ over $y$ from $\mathbf{j}$: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{3}{8} = 20.56^{\circ}$, and $90 - 20.56 = 69.44$ is the angle with $\mathbf{i}$.

prompt: With $\mathbf{i}$ due east and $\mathbf{j}$ due north, which calculation gives a bearing?
options: $\tan^{-1}$ of the east component over the north component
$\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
$90$ plus $\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
answer: $\tan^{-1}$ of the east component over the north component
explain: A bearing starts at north and turns clockwise, as step 3 of See it did, so it is the angle with $\mathbf{j}$: north is beside the angle and east is opposite it, giving east over north. North over east is the angle above east instead, and adding $90$ measures from the wrong axis.

twin.prompt: With $\mathbf{i}$ due east and $\mathbf{j}$ due north, which calculation gives the angle a displacement makes with the east direction?
options: $\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
$\tan^{-1}$ of the east component over the north component
$90$ minus $\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
twin.answer: $\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
twin.explain: Measured from east, the east component is beside the angle and the north component is opposite it, so the fraction is north over east: the formula on the sheet.

optionNotes.option: $\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
optionNotes.why: That is the angle up from east, the formula printed on the sheet, but a bearing is measured from north.

optionNotes.option: $90$ plus $\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
optionNotes.why: Adding 90 swings the angle from east on past north; a bearing is simply the angle from north itself.

caption: A vector with a negative $\mathbf{j}$ component points below the x-axis; its angle comes from the sizes.

md: **Build the vector first.** The magnitude is usually of something you make: $\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{d}$ (Summer 2024), $\mathbf{r} + \mathbf{w}$ (Summer 2025), the resultant of three forces (Summer 2026), or a velocity from $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t$ (Summer 2019). Collect the $\mathbf{i}$ parts and the $\mathbf{j}$ parts, then square.

**A negative component.** The angle with the positive x-axis uses the sizes of the components; the sketch says which side of the axis it lies. **Speed** is the magnitude of the velocity: in Summer 2019 most candidates stopped at the velocity.

stem: $\mathbf{p} = (9\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{q} = (4\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ N. Calculate the magnitude of $\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}$ and the angle it makes with the positive x-axis.

steps.decision: Subtract the i parts and the j parts separately: 9 − 4 and 2 − 5. This line earns the first method mark.
Square each component, add and root: the minus sign vanishes in the square.
Use the sizes, 3 over 5; the minus sign on the j component says the arrow points below the axis, as the sketch shows.

prompt: $\mathbf{r} = (2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{s} = (6\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j})$ N. What is the magnitude of $\mathbf{r} + \mathbf{s}$, to 2 decimal places, in newtons?
explain: Build the vector first, as step 1 of See it did: $\mathbf{r} + \mathbf{s} = 8\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}$. Then $\sqrt{8^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{68} = 8.25$ N. Adding the magnitudes of r and s separately gives a different length.

twin.prompt: $\mathbf{u} = (\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{w} = (5\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ N. What is the magnitude of $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}$, to 2 decimal places, in newtons?
twin.explain: Add the parts first: $6\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}$, then $\sqrt{6^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{40} = 6.32$ N.

md:
Find a magnitude: square the components, add, root; a minus sign makes no difference.
Find the angle with $\mathbf{i}$ as $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{y}{x}$, using the sizes of the components.
Find the angle with $\mathbf{j}$ as $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x}{y}$, and check the two add to $90^{\circ}$.
Give a bearing as the angle with $\mathbf{j}$ when $\mathbf{j}$ points north.
Build the vector first, and give a speed as the magnitude of a velocity.

These parts close a vectors question, 2 or 3 marks each, after a part that builds the vector (Summer 2019, 2024, 2025 and 2026). The first mark is the substitution written down, the square root or the inverse tangent with the numbers in; the last is the value to 2 decimal places. Stuck? Sketch the triangle and mark the angle you want.
